full_name: GC and Others v Commission nationale de l'informatique et des libertés (CNIL)
topic: Sensitive data in search engine results
holding:

2. The prohibition on processing special categories of data (Art 8 Directive 95/46) applies to search engine operators
3. Exceptions may apply: data manifestly made public by the data subject, or substantial public interest
4. A HEIGHTENED balancing test applies to delisting requests involving special categories of data
facts: Four individuals requested Google to delist search results linking to webpages that disclosed information about their criminal proceedings, political affiliations, and religious beliefs. Search engine operators must apply the stricter special categories regime, not just the general rules
Right to delisting is STRENGTHENED for results involving sensitive data (health, criminal, political, religious)
Public interest in access is weighed more strictly against privacy when sensitive data is at stake
The search engine operator bears responsibility regardless of whether it intentionally processed the sensitive aspects

Processing of criminal records data and health information by search engines significantly restricted

name: Österreichische Post II
full_name: Österreichische Post AG v RW
topic: Right of access — scope and modalities
holding:
1. Where personal data has been or will be disclosed to recipients, the controller must provide the SPECIFIC IDENTITY of those recipients upon request
2. Providing merely the 'categories of recipients' is only an alternative where the identity of specific recipients cannot be provided, or where the data has not yet been disclosed
3. The right of access must be interpreted broadly to enable the data subject to effectively exercise other GDPR rights (rectification, erasure, objection)
facts: RW requested from Österreichische Post (Austrian Post) access to his personal data under GDPR Article 15, including the identity of specific recipients to whom his data had been disclosed. Österreichische Post provided only the categories of recipients, not their specific identities. The Austrian Supreme Court referred whether Art 15(1)(c) requires disclosure of specific recipient identities.
key_legal_points: Specific recipient identities must be provided under Art 15(1)(c), not just categories
Categories of recipients are the fallback, not the default — specific identification is the primary obligation
Right of access is foundational: it enables informed exercise of all other data subject rights
The controller bears the obligation unless providing specific identities is impossible or the disclosure has not yet occurred
practical_impact: Controllers must track and be prepared to disclose specific third-party recipients of personal data
Data mapping and recipient tracking systems became essential for compliance
Data subjects gained more effective oversight of who has access to their data
Increased the transparency requirements for data sharing and disclosure practices
ai_relevance: Organisations using AI services must be able to identify specifically which AI providers received personal data
Data subjects can demand to know which AI training pipelines or third-party AI services received their data
AI data brokers and aggregators are specific recipients that must be disclosed under Art 15(1)(c)
Automated data sharing pipelines feeding into AI systems must be documented for access request compliance
Operative Part (from judgment):

Article 15(1)(c) of Regulation (EU) 2016/679 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 27 April 2016 on the protection of natural persons with regard to the processing of personal data and on the free movement of such data, and repealing Directive 95/46/EC (General Data Protection Regulation), must be interpreted as meaning that the data subject’s right of access to the personal data concerning him or her, provided for by that provision, entails, where those data have been or will be disclosed to recipients, an obligation on the part of the controller to provide the data subject with the actual identity of those recipients, unless it is impossible to identify those recipients or the controller demonstrates that the data subject’s requests for access are manifestly unfounded or excessive within the meaning of Article 12(5) of Regulation 2016/679, in which cases the controller may indicate to the data subject only the categories of recipient in question.

Topic: Right of access — scope and modalities

Provisions Interpreted: GDPR Articles 12, 15(1)(c)

Facts:

name: SS SIA
full_name: SIA 'SS' v Valsts ieņēmumu dienests
topic: Legitimate interest — scope and proportionality
holding:
1. A tax authority's request for personal data must comply with the data minimisation principle under GDPR
2. The legitimate interests basis (Art 6(1)(f)) requires a three-part test: legitimate interest, necessity, and balancing against data subject rights
3. When a public authority processes data based on a legal obligation (Art 6(1)(c) or (e)), legitimate interest (Art 6(1)(f)) is not the appropriate basis
4. Data requested by a tax authority must be adequate, relevant and limited to what is necessary for the tax verification purpose
facts: The Latvian tax authority requested a taxi company (SIA SS) to provide personal data of its drivers, including detailed trip records, to verify tax compliance. The company challenged the scope of data requested as excessive. The Latvian court referred questions about the proportionality of data disclosure to tax authorities and the scope of the legitimate interest legal basis.
key_legal_points: Public authorities should rely on Art 6(1)(c) or (e), NOT Art 6(1)(f) — legitimate interest basis is not available to public authorities for their core tasks
Even when data disclosure is mandated by law, the underlying legislation must respect data minimisation
Proportionality applies to scope: bulk disclosure of all records may be excessive if targeted requests suffice
Data subjects' reasonable expectations are a factor in the balancing test
practical_impact: Limits the scope of data that tax and regulatory authorities can demand from businesses
Organisations can push back against overbroad data requests from public authorities
Reinforces that legitimate interest is not a carte blanche — strict necessity and balancing required
ai_relevance: AI systems processing personal data under 'legitimate interest' must implement the three-part test (purpose, necessity, balancing)
Bulk data collection for AI training cannot be justified under legitimate interest without rigorous proportionality analysis
AI-powered tax compliance systems requesting data must respect data minimisation and purpose limitation
Data subjects' reasonable expectations limit AI profiling justified under legitimate interest
Operative Part (from judgment):

1. The provisions of Regulation (EU) 2016/679 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 27 April 2016 on the protection of natural persons with regard to the processing of personal data and on the free movement of such data, and repealing Directive 95/46/EC (General Data Protection Regulation) must be interpreted as meaning that the collection by the tax authorities of a Member State from an economic operator of information involving a significant amount of personal data is subject to the requirements of that regulation, in particular those set out in Article 5(1) thereof. 2. The provisions of Regulation 2016/679 must be interpreted as meaning that the tax authorities of a Member State may not derogate from the provisions of Article 5(1) of that regulation where such a right has not been granted to them by a legislative measure within the meaning of Article 23(1) thereof. 3. The provisions of Regulation 2016/679 must be interpreted as not precluding the tax authorities of a Member State from requiring a provider of internet advertisement services to disclose to them information relating to taxpayers who have published advertisements in one of the sections of its internet portal, provided, in particular, that those data are necessary in the light of the specific purposes for which they are collected and that the period to which the data collection relates does not exceed the period strictly necessary to achieve the objective of general interest sought.

name: Vyriausioji
full_name: Vyriausioji tarnybinės etikos komisija v OT
topic: DPA powers and public transparency obligations
holding:
1. National legislation requiring online publication of the personal data (including names of spouses/partners) of public officials constitutes an interference with Articles 7 and 8 of the Charter
2. Such interference must be proportionate: the publication must be limited to what is strictly necessary for anti-corruption and transparency objectives
3. National legislation must provide clear and precise rules on scope and application of the transparency measure
4. Publication of a public official's partner's personal data online may be disproportionate where less intrusive means exist
facts: A Lithuanian ethics commission was required by national law to publish online declarations of private interests by public officials, including data about cohabitants and partners. OT, a director of an environmental protection body, challenged the publication of his partner's personal data. The Lithuanian courts referred questions to the CJEU on proportionality of mandatory transparency measures.
key_legal_points: Mandatory public transparency measures must be balanced against data protection rights — no automatic override
Data minimisation applies even in the context of legitimate anti-corruption and transparency objectives
The principle of proportionality requires assessment of whether less intrusive measures could achieve the same goal
Online publication is more intrusive than making data available for inspection in physical offices
GDPR Article 9 (sensitive data) may be engaged where published data reveals aspects of private life
practical_impact: Governments must review transparency legislation for GDPR proportionality compliance
Online publication of public officials' data must be assessed against data minimisation principles
Less intrusive alternatives (e.g., physical inspection, redacted versions) must be considered
ai_relevance: AI-powered transparency and open-data platforms publishing officials' personal data must respect proportionality
Automated disclosure systems (e.g., AI-driven FOIA responses) must implement data minimisation checks
AI scraping of publicly available government registers for profiling is not automatically lawful
AI anti-corruption tools processing personal data of officials and associates must respect data protection

Topic: DPA powers and public transparency obligations

Facts:
A Lithuanian ethics commission was required by national law to publish online declarations of private interests by public officials, including data about cohabitants and partners. name: Österreichische Post
full_name: Österreichische Post AG v UI
topic: Non-material damages under GDPR Article 82
holding:
1. Article 82 GDPR requires THREE cumulative conditions: (1) a GDPR infringement, (2) damage suffered, and (3) a causal link between them
2. There is NO de minimis threshold for non-material damage — even minor distress can give rise to compensation
3. However, the mere infringement of GDPR provisions is NOT sufficient alone — actual damage must be demonstrated
4. National courts determine the amount of compensation according to domestic rules, subject to EU principles of equivalence and effectiveness
facts: Österreichische Post (Austrian Post) used an algorithm to assess the political affinities of the Austrian population based on socio-demographic criteria, assigning political party affinity scores without consent. UI, a data subject, claimed non-material damages for distress caused by the processing. The Austrian Supreme Court referred questions on the threshold for GDPR damages claims.
key_legal_points: GDPR Article 82 has a COMPENSATORY function, not a punitive one — damages must correspond to actual damage suffered
No minimum severity threshold: 'mere upset' or distress can constitute non-material damage if proven
But a bare GDPR violation without demonstrated damage does not trigger compensation — damage is a separate condition
National procedural rules apply to calculation of damages, but must not make it excessively difficult to obtain compensation
practical_impact: Opened the door to widespread non-material damages claims across the EU for GDPR violations
Organisations face financial exposure for distress caused by any GDPR breach, however minor
No minimum threshold means even small-scale privacy violations can result in damages awards
Mass damages claims and class actions for data protection violations became more viable
ai_relevance: AI profiling that causes distress (e.g., political profiling, discriminatory scoring) can trigger damages claims
Non-material damage claims can arise from AI-driven processing that infringes GDPR, even without financial loss
Algorithmic bias causing emotional distress is actionable under Art 82 — no minimum severity
AI developers face damages liability if their systems process personal data in violation of GDPR and cause distress
Operative Part (from judgment):

1. Article 82(1) of Regulation (EU) 2016/679 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 27 April 2016 on the protection of natural persons with regard to the processing of personal data and on the free movement of such data, and repealing Directive 95/46/EC (General Data Protection Regulation) must be interpreted as meaning that the mere infringement of the provisions of that regulation is not sufficient to confer a right to compensation. 2. Article 82(1) of Regulation 2016/679 must be interpreted as precluding a national rule or practice which makes compensation for non-material damage, within the meaning of that provision, subject to the condition that the damage suffered by the data subject has reached a certain degree of seriousness. 3. Article 82 of Regulation 2016/679 must be interpreted as meaning that for the purposes of determining the amount of damages payable under the right to compensation enshrined in that article, national courts must apply the domestic rules of each Member State relating to the extent of financial compensation, provided that the principles of equivalence and effectiveness of EU law are complied with.

name: Schrems II
full_name: Data Protection Commissioner v Facebook Ireland Ltd and Maximillian Schrems
topic: International data transfers
holding:
1. The EU-US Privacy Shield adequacy decision (Decision 2016/1250) is INVALID
2. Standard Contractual Clauses (Decision 2010/87) remain VALID in principle
3. Data exporters must verify that the law of the third country ensures adequate protection BEFORE each transfer
4. Supplementary measures may be needed where the law of the third country impairs the effectiveness of SCCs
5. DPAs are REQUIRED to suspend or prohibit transfers where SCCs cannot be complied with in the third country
facts: Max Schrems complained that his personal data was transferred by Facebook Ireland to Facebook Inc. in the US, where it was subject to NSA and FBI surveillance programmes (FISA Section 702, Executive Order 12333). He challenged the validity of Standard Contractual Clauses (SCCs) and the EU-US Privacy Shield adequacy decision before the Irish Data Protection Commissioner, who referred the matter to the High Court, which in turn referred questions to the CJEU.
key_legal_points: Adequacy standard requires 'essentially equivalent' protection, not identical
US surveillance laws (FISA 702, EO 12333) are incompatible with EU fundamental rights (Arts 7, 8, 47 Charter)
Controller must perform a case-by-case assessment of third country law before each transfer
DPA has an obligation to act when SCCs are not complied with, not merely discretion
Privacy Shield Ombudsperson mechanism does not satisfy Art 47 Charter (right to effective remedy)
Bulk collection of communications data under EO 12333 not limited to what is strictly necessary
practical_impact: All US data transfers post-Schrems II require Transfer Impact Assessments (TIAs)
Supplementary technical measures (encryption, pseudonymisation) became essential for third-country transfers
Led to adoption of the EU-US Data Privacy Framework (2023) as replacement adequacy mechanism
EDPB issued Recommendations 01/2020 on supplementary measures
Organisations had to map and document all international data flows
ai_relevance: AI models trained on personal data transferred from EU to US must comply with Schrems II requirements
Cloud-hosted AI processing in the US falls squarely under international transfer rules
Model weights derived from personal data may itself constitute a data transfer
AI-as-a-Service providers must implement supplementary measures (encryption in transit/at rest, pseudonymisation)
Transfer Impact Assessments needed for AI training pipelines involving cross-border data flows
Operative Part (from judgment):

1. Article 2(1) and (2) of Regulation (EU) 2016/679 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 27 April 2016 on the protection of natural persons with regard to the processing of personal data and on the free movement of such data, and repealing Directive 95/46/EC (General Data Protection Regulation), must be interpreted as meaning that that regulation applies to the transfer of personal data for commercial purposes by an economic operator established in a Member State to another economic operator established in a third country, irrespective of whether, at the time of that transfer or thereafter, that data is liable to be processed by the authorities of the third country in question for the purposes of public security, defence and State security. 2. holding:

2. The controller bears the BURDEN OF PROOF to demonstrate that its security measures were appropriate under Art 32 GDPR

name: Fashion ID
full_name: Fashion ID GmbH & Co. KG v Verbraucherzentrale NRW eV
topic: Joint controllership for social plugins
holding:
1. A website operator embedding a third-party social plugin is a JOINT CONTROLLER with the plugin provider
2. Joint controllership is LIMITED to the operations for which the website operator actually determines purposes and means (collection and transmission), NOT for subsequent processing by the plugin provider
3. The website operator must obtain consent or establish another legal basis BEFORE data is transmitted to the plugin provider
4. Consumer protection associations may bring representative actions against data protection violations
facts: Fashion ID, a German online clothing retailer, embedded a Facebook 'Like' button on its website. This caused visitors' browsers to transmit personal data (IP address, browser string, page URL) to Facebook Ireland, even if visitors did not click the button or have a Facebook account. The German consumer association Verbraucherzentrale NRW brought proceedings.
key_legal_points: Joint controllership applies proportionally — each controller responsible only for the processing stages they determine
Website operator is responsible for consent/legal basis at the point of embed-triggered data collection
Consent must be obtained BEFORE the plugin loads and transmits data
Legitimate interest (Art 7(f)) could also serve as legal basis but requires proper balancing
Consumer organisations have standing to bring data protection claims
practical_impact: Websites must obtain consent before loading third-party tracking elements (social buttons, analytics, ads)
Led to widespread adoption of two-click solutions for social media embeds
Joint controller agreements with platform providers became necessary
Changed how third-party scripts and SDKs are deployed on websites
ai_relevance: AI widgets, chatbots, and APIs embedded on websites create joint controller scenarios with the AI provider
Websites integrating third-party AI services (recommendations, chatbots) must analyse joint controllership
AI analytics tools embedded via JavaScript/pixels follow the same rules — consent before loading
AI-powered ad tech and personalisation embeds require prior consent mechanisms
Operative Part (from judgment):

1. Articles 22 to 24 of Directive 95/46/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 24 October 1995 on the protection of individuals with regard to the processing of personal data and on the free movement of such data must be interpreted as not precluding national legislation which allows consumer-protection associations to bring or defend legal proceedings against a person allegedly responsible for an infringement of the protection of personal data. 2. The operator of a website, such as Fashion ID GmbH & Co. KG, that embeds on that website a social plugin causing the browser of a visitor to that website to request content from the provider of that plugin and, to that end, to transmit to that provider personal data of the visitor can be considered to be a controller, within the meaning of Article 2(d) of Directive 95/46. That liability is, however, limited to the operation or set of operations involving the processing of personal data in respect of which it actually determines the purposes and means, that is to say, the collection and disclosure by transmission of the data at issue. 3. In a situation such as that at issue in the main proceedings, in which the operator of a website embeds on that website a social plugin causing the browser of a visitor to that website to request content from the provider of that plugin and, to that end, to transmit to that provider personal data of the visitor, it is necessary that that operator and that provider each pursue a legitimate interest, within the meaning of Article 7(f) of Directive 95/46, through those processing operations in order for those operations to be justified in respect of each of them. 4. Article 2(h) and Article 7(a) of Directive 95/46 must be interpreted as meaning that, in a situation such as that at issue in the main proceedings, in which the operator of a website embeds on that website a social plugin causing the browser of a visitor to that website to request content from the provider of that plugin and, to that end, to transmit to that provider personal data of the visitor, the consent referred to in those provisions must be obtained by that operator only with regard to the operation or set of operations involving the processing of personal data in respect of which that operator determines the purposes and means. In addition, Article 10 of that directive must be interpreted as meaning that, in such a situation, the duty to inform laid down in that provision is incumbent also on that operator, but the information that the latter must provide to the data subject need relate only to the operation or set of operations involving the processing of personal data in respect of which that operator actually determines the purposes and means.

name: Schrems III
full_name: Maximillian Schrems v Meta Platforms Ireland Ltd
topic: Data minimisation and purpose limitation for social networks
holding:
1. The data minimisation principle (Art 5(1)(c)) prohibits the aggregation and analysis of ALL personal data for targeted advertising without temporal or content limitation
2. The fact that a data subject has manifestly made data public (Art 9(2)(e)) does NOT authorise unlimited processing of that data
3. Public disclosure of sensitive data for one context (e.g., a panel discussion) does not permit processing in a different context (e.g., targeted advertising)
4. Social network operators cannot justify unlimited data collection and combination under 'contractual necessity' (Art 6(1)(b))
facts: Maximillian Schrems brought proceedings against Meta Platforms Ireland regarding Facebook's processing of his personal data, including targeting of advertisements based on his sexual orientation, which he had disclosed publicly at a panel discussion. The Vienna Regional Court referred questions on data minimisation, purpose limitation, and whether public disclosure of sensitive data permits unlimited processing.
key_legal_points: Data minimisation limits both the scope of data collected and the purposes for which it may be aggregated
'Manifestly made public' under Art 9(2)(e) is context-dependent — public disclosure for one purpose does not mean consent to all processing
Purpose limitation prevents repurposing of publicly shared data for unrelated commercial uses
Social network processing for advertising must have a distinct legal basis from the core service provision
practical_impact: Limits the ability of social media platforms to aggregate user data without boundaries for ad targeting
Public statements by individuals cannot be used as blanket authorisation for profiling and ad targeting
Stricter interpretation of contextual integrity in data processing decisions
ai_relevance: AI training on publicly available personal data is NOT automatically lawful under Art 9(2)(e) — context matters
AI systems must respect data minimisation when aggregating personal data for model training or profiling
AI-driven ad targeting using sensitive data inferred or disclosed publicly must have a proper legal basis per context
Large language models training on social media data containing sensitive self-disclosures face Art 9 constraints
Operative Part (from judgment):

1. Article 5(1)(c) of Regulation (EU) 2016/679 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 27 April 2016 on the protection of natural persons with regard to the processing of personal data and on the free movement of such data, and repealing Directive 95/46/EC (General Data Protection Regulation), must be interpreted as meaning that the principle of data minimisation provided for therein precludes any personal data obtained by a controller, such as the operator of an online social network platform, from the data subject or third parties and collected either on or outside that platform, from being aggregated, analysed and processed for the purposes of targeted advertising without restriction as to time and without distinction as to type of data. 2. full_name: SCHUFA Holding AG (Scoring)
topic: Credit scoring as automated individual decision-making under Art 22
holding:
1. The production of a CREDIT SCORE (probability value) by a credit reference agency constitutes an 'automated individual decision' under Article 22(1) GDPR when it SIGNIFICANTLY AFFECTS the data subject
2. Art 22 is not limited to the FINAL decision (e.g., credit denial) — it also covers PREPARATORY automated acts that predetermine the outcome
3. Art 22 provides a general PROHIBITION on such decisions, subject to the exceptions in Art 22(2)
4. National legislation permitting credit scoring must ensure adequate safeguards including the right to human intervention, to express a point of view, and to contest the decision
facts: SCHUFA Holding AG, Germany's largest credit reference agency, calculated credit scores (probability values) used by banks and other lenders to decide whether to grant credit. A data subject was denied a mobile phone contract based on a low SCHUFA score. The Hessian DPA found no violation. The Wiesbaden Administrative Court referred questions on whether automated scoring constitutes a decision under Art 22 GDPR.
key_legal_points: Credit scoring that effectively predetermines outcomes = automated individual decision-making under Art 22 GDPR
Art 22 applies not just to the final decision-maker but to upstream automated preparatory acts that substantially drive the outcome
The prohibition in Art 22(1) is a RIGHT of the data subject, not merely a general prohibition
Must provide: meaningful information about the logic involved, right to human intervention, right to express views and contest
National exceptions under Art 22(2)(b) must include appropriate safeguards
practical_impact: Credit reference agencies across the EU must ensure Art 22 compliance for automated scoring
Any automated preparation of decisions that predetermines outcomes falls under Art 22 — not just the final click
Transparency about scoring logic is a legal requirement — 'meaningful information' must be provided
Banks relying on third-party automated scores are also subject to Art 22 obligations
ai_relevance: AI-based credit scoring, risk assessment, and automated decision systems fall directly under Art 22 GDPR
AI model explainability becomes a LEGAL REQUIREMENT — controllers must provide 'meaningful information about the logic involved'
The 'preparatory act' doctrine means AI systems producing scores/recommendations used in human decisions are also covered
AI-as-a-Service scoring platforms (creditworthiness, insurance risk, tenant screening) face Art 22 compliance obligations
Algorithmic transparency and right to contestation apply to all AI-driven individual assessments with significant effects

topic: Health data processing and legal privilege
holding:

The German court referred questions on the scope of the health data processing exception and Art 82 damages.

Unlawful processing of health data gives rise to non-material damages — heightened sensitivity increases likelihood of genuine distress

topic: Data protection by design / mobile contact-tracing apps
holding:
1. An entity that initiates and defines the parameters of a data processing project can be a controller even if it does not directly process data or formally commission the processing
2. Joint controllership arises where multiple entities jointly determine purposes and means, even without a formal arrangement
3. The data minimisation principle (Art 5(1)(c)) requires that personal data collected be adequate, relevant, and limited to what is necessary
4. A controller may be fined under Art 83 GDPR even if it did not specifically authorise the excessive data collection, where it failed to exercise sufficient oversight
facts: Lithuania's National Public Health Centre (NVSC) oversaw development of a COVID-19 contact-tracing mobile app (KARANTINAS) that collected excessive personal data beyond what was necessary for contact tracing. The Lithuanian DPA fined NVSC and the app developer. NVSC argued it was not the controller. Questions were referred to the CJEU on joint controllership, data minimisation, and fining of public bodies.
key_legal_points: Data protection by design (Art 25) must be integrated from the conception stage of any system
Joint controllers exist even absent a formal Art 26 arrangement — de facto joint determination of purposes/means suffices
Data minimisation is violated when an app collects data categories beyond what its stated purpose requires
Public authorities can be fined under GDPR if national law permits — controller responsibility extends to oversight failures
The GDPR applies fully to public health emergency measures — no general pandemic exception
practical_impact: Contact-tracing and health surveillance apps must implement strict data minimisation from the design phase
Public bodies procuring IT systems/apps remain controllers responsible for GDPR compliance of the resulting system
Even emergency measures and public health deployments must respect GDPR principles throughout
Formal joint controller agreements (Art 26) should be concluded before processing begins
ai_relevance: AI-powered contact-tracing and health monitoring systems must implement data protection by design
AI systems collecting data for public health must respect data minimisation — no excessive collection for 'potential future AI use'
Entities commissioning AI development remain controllers even if they lack technical AI expertise
Joint controllership implications for AI procurement: commissioner + developer may both be controllers
AI systems deployed during emergencies (pandemics, crises) are not exempt from GDPR requirements
Operative Part (from judgment):

1. Article 4(7) of Regulation (EU) 2016/679 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 27 April 2016 on the protection of natural persons with regard to the processing of personal data and on the free movement of such data, and repealing Directive 95/46/EC (General Data Protection Regulation), must be interpreted as meaning that an entity which has entrusted an undertaking with the development of a mobile IT application and which has, in that context, participated in the determination of the purposes and means of the processing of personal data carried out through that application may be regarded as a controller, within the meaning of that provision, even if that entity has not itself performed any processing operations in respect of such data, has not expressly agreed to the performance of specific operations for such processing or to that mobile application being made available to the public, and has not acquired the abovementioned mobile application, unless, prior to that application being made available to the public, that entity expressly objected to such making available and to the resulting processing of personal data. 2. Article 4(7) and Article 26(1) of Regulation 2016/679 must be interpreted as meaning that the classification of two entities as joint controllers does not require that there be an arrangement between those entities regarding the determination of the purposes and means of the processing of personal data in question; nor does it require that there be an arrangement laying down the terms of the joint control. 3. name: Deutsche Wohnen
full_name: Deutsche Wohnen SE v Staatsanwaltschaft Berlin
topic: Direct corporate liability for GDPR fines
holding:
1. GDPR fines can be imposed DIRECTLY on legal persons/undertakings, without requiring identification of a specific natural person who committed the infringement
2. Corporate fault is sufficient: where the controller 'ought to have been aware' of the infringement, a fine can be imposed
3. The concept of 'undertaking' in Art 83 GDPR follows the EU competition law concept — parent companies can be liable for subsidiaries
4. National legal traditions requiring identification of an individual perpetrator cannot undermine the effectiveness of GDPR fines
facts: The Berlin DPA fined Deutsche Wohnen (a major housing company) €14.5 million for storing tenants' personal data longer than necessary without a proper retention policy. German courts questioned whether GDPR fines could be imposed directly on legal persons (under German law, corporate criminal liability was limited). The CJEU was asked whether GDPR allows direct fining of undertakings.
key_legal_points: Direct corporate liability model: companies can be fined without proving fault of a specific employee
A controller that negligently fails to implement proper data protection measures is liable — strict liability is not required but negligence suffices
'Undertaking' concept from EU competition law imported into GDPR — group-level responsibility possible
National procedural rules cannot render GDPR fining powers ineffective
Turnover-based fines (up to 4% of worldwide annual turnover) calculated at group/undertaking level
practical_impact: Removed legal obstacles to corporate GDPR fines in jurisdictions requiring individual fault attribution
DPAs across the EU can fine companies directly without identifying which employee was responsible
Parent companies face liability for GDPR infringements by subsidiaries within their corporate group
Significantly strengthened the deterrence effect of GDPR enforcement in all Member States
ai_relevance: Companies deploying AI systems that violate GDPR face direct corporate fines without need to identify the responsible developer
Corporate groups deploying AI across subsidiaries face group-level fine exposure based on worldwide turnover
AI governance failures (lack of DPIAs, inadequate oversight) can lead to corporate fines on negligence grounds
Automated processing violations are attributable to the corporate controller, not individual technicians
Operative Part (from judgment):

1. Article 58(2)(i) and Article 83(1) to (6) of Regulation (EU) 2016/679 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 27 April 2016 on the protection of natural persons with regard to the processing of personal data and on the free movement of such data, and repealing Directive 95/46/EC (General Data Protection Regulation), must be interpreted as precluding national legislation under which an administrative fine may be imposed on a legal person in its capacity as controller in respect of an infringement referred to in Article 83(4) to (6) only in so far as that infringement has previously been attributed to an identified natural person. 2. Article 83 of Regulation 2016/679 must be interpreted as meaning that an administrative fine may be imposed pursuant to that provision only where it is established that the controller, which is both a legal person and an undertaking, intentionally or negligently committed an infringement referred to in Article 83(4) to (6) thereof.
